artifact.title: Personal expense tracker: storage approach review

nodes.title: Decision context
nodes.text: Choose the default storage architecture for a personal expense tracker. This review assumes one primary user, sensitive financial data, a desire for reliable backups, and possible use across more than one device. It compares product and operational tradeoffs only; it does not implement the tracker.

nodes.title: At-a-glance comparison
nodes.text: With seamless phone-and-laptop access now mandatory at launch, cloud sync becomes the better launch fit; local-only still minimizes data exposure and infrastructure but cannot meet the core access requirement without manual transfer.

nodes.title: Local-only: benefits
nodes.text: Keeps sensitive spending data under direct user control. Works without an account or connection. Reduces the initial build, testing, compliance, and support surface. Offers predictable behavior because there is no distributed state to reconcile. Can still support explicit encrypted exports and platform-level device backups.

nodes.title: Local-only: risks
nodes.text: With seamless phone-and-laptop access required at launch, local-only is not just inconvenient across devices; it fails a stated launch requirement unless a sync mechanism is added. Its remaining major risk is unrecoverable loss when a device is lost, damaged, reset, or corrupted. Mitigate with encrypted export/import, backup reminders, atomic writes, schema migrations, recovery testing, and platform-appropriate encryption.

data.mitigation: Encrypted export/import, backup reminders, atomic writes, schema migrations, recovery testing, and platform-appropriate encryption still reduce loss risk, but they do not provide seamless cross-device access.

nodes.title: Cloud sync: benefits
nodes.text: Makes records available across phones, tablets, and the web. Central backup can make device replacement and recovery easier. Enables future shared budgets, receipt processing, or server-side insights. A well-designed offline-first client can preserve day-to-day use during temporary connectivity loss.

nodes.title: Cloud sync: risks
nodes.text: Cloud sync is now required to satisfy launch scope, so its security and operational risks are accepted responsibilities rather than optional future complexity. Financial records become a high-value remote target, and sync can introduce duplicate, stale, or conflicting edits that damage user trust. Authentication, authorization, encryption, retention, deletion, incident response, account recovery, availability, and cost all become product concerns.

data.mitigation: Use a mature identity provider, least-privilege access, encryption, auditable deletion, conflict-safe data modeling, idempotent sync, clear offline/online semantics, monitoring, cost controls, and tested restore and account-recovery procedures.

nodes.title: Recommendation
nodes.text: Choose cloud sync for launch because seamless phone-and-laptop access is now mandatory and local-only cannot meet that requirement without introducing a sync mechanism. Accept the larger security and operational burden deliberately: use offline-first behavior for resilience, strong access controls and encryption for sensitive financial data, conflict-safe synchronization, and tested backup, restore, and account-recovery flows. Preserve a local cache and export path so the user retains offline usability and recovery options.

nodes.title: Storage architecture decision
nodes.text: Select the approach that should define the initial product scope.
